catalog_quote: The stress falls generally on the first syllable in a multisyllabic word. Therefore, it often gives a clue to word boundaries or syntactic relationships between parts of an utterance. audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict, initial) rests on the only reference grammar of the language, which has an explicit stress section; we hold the full thesis and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated section and pages (thesis pp.25-26 = PDF pp.42-43). Osumi's description gives no word-level exceptions (prefixes count as first syllable; long vowel = one syllable; hedges concern sentence rhythm), so 'fixed initial' is a faithful reading. Glottolog lists no competing grammar or phonology; the one other primary source, Grace's 1976 dictionary, was downloaded and is silent on stress. Only cosmetic improvement possible: reword the domain locator to cite the 1990 thesis pagination (or verify the 1995 book's) since the copy we hold is the thesis, not the UH Press edition.
